clinicalPearls: A rare, diffuse hardening of the skin and subcutaneous fat affecting critically ill, usually premature or low-birth-weight neonates in the first week of life.
The skin becomes cold, board-like, waxy and immobile, spreading rapidly from the buttocks and lower limbs to involve most of the body, sparing the palms, soles and genitalia.
It is almost always a marker of severe underlying illness such as sepsis, dehydration, hypothermia, hypoxia or congenital malformation, rather than a primary skin disease.
Unlike subcutaneous fat necrosis of the newborn, affected infants are gravely unwell and the induration is diffuse rather than nodular.
The rigid skin restricts respiration and feeding, compounding the underlying condition.
Histology shows widened fibrous septa and needle-shaped clefts within enlarged adipocytes, with little or no inflammatory infiltrate and minimal fat necrosis.
Management is directed at the underlying illness, aggressive supportive care, warming, correction of fluid and electrolyte disturbances and treatment of sepsis.
Mortality is high and correlates with the severity of the precipitating illness rather than the skin changes themselves.
reference.pathophysiology: Sclerema neonatorum reflects the physicochemical vulnerability of neonatal subcutaneous fat, which has a high ratio of saturated to unsaturated fatty acids and thus a high melting point. In a critically ill, hypothermic and hypoperfused infant, this fat solidifies and crystallises, producing diffuse induration. Enzymatic defects in fatty-acid mobilisation and impaired thermoregulation are thought to contribute. Histologically there is little inflammation or true necrosis; instead adipocytes enlarge and contain needle-shaped crystal clefts, and the fibrous septa thicken. The process is best understood as a physical solidification of fat in a decompensating infant, so the condition is essentially an epiphenomenon of severe systemic illness.
additionalDifferentials: subcutaneous fat necrosis of the newborn
neonatal sepsis with oedema and induration
additionalInvestigations: full septic screen including blood cultures, lumbar puncture and cultures as indicated
full blood count, C-reactive protein and coagulation studies
serum electrolytes, glucose, urea and creatinine
blood gas analysis for hypoxia and acidosis
skin biopsy for histopathology when diagnosis is uncertain (wide septa, crystal clefts, scant inflammation)
chest radiograph and other imaging directed at the underlying illness
redFlags: rapidly spreading induration in a hypothermic, hypotensive or septic neonate
respiratory compromise from restricted chest-wall movement
inability to feed or maintain temperature despite supportive measures
reference.prognosis: The prognosis is poor, with high mortality driven by the severity of the underlying illness; survival depends on prompt and effective treatment of the precipitating condition rather than of the skin changes.
pitfalls: Regarding the skin hardening as the primary problem instead of a sign of critical systemic illness.
Confusing it with the far more benign subcutaneous fat necrosis of the newborn.
Delaying sepsis evaluation and empirical treatment while investigating the skin.
Underestimating the respiratory impact of diffuse cutaneous rigidity.
Attributing induration to primary scleroderma in a neonate.
references: Rook's Textbook of Dermatology, current edition
Textbook of Neonatal Dermatology, current edition
management: Treat the underlying critical illness aggressively — sepsis, dehydration, hypothermia and hypoxia — since outcome depends on this rather than on the skin
Give broad-spectrum intravenous antibiotics for suspected sepsis after taking cultures, guided by the septic screen
Provide intensive supportive care with careful rewarming, correction of fluid and electrolyte disturbance and haemodynamic support in a neonatal intensive care setting
Support respiration, including mechanical ventilation, as the rigid skin restricts chest movement
Maintain nutrition and correct hypoglycaemia and acidosis
Monitor core temperature, blood gases and coagulation, treating disseminated intravascular coagulation as needed
Involve neonatology early and discuss the guarded prognosis with the family given the high mortality
